analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from cutting retirees' health benefits after they retire and requires restoring cuts already made.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House committee without a hearing or vote; its sponsor and 79 cosponsors never got it to the floor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the federal pension law (ERISA) to prohibit group health plans from canceling or reducing the health benefits of people after they retire — including raising their out-of-pocket costs or limiting their access to care. Plans that had already cut benefits after retirement would have to restore them, unless they could prove doing so would cause substantial business hardship. To help employers pay for restoration, it would create a $5 billion federal loan guarantee program, and the Labor Secretary could fine violators up to $1,000 per person per violation.
analysis.who_benefits: Retired workers whose employer-sponsored health coverage was cut or canceled after they retired. Many were retirees with preexisting conditions who could not buy comparable individual coverage without depleting their savings; the bill would let them claim back the benefits taken away, and would prevent future cuts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retirees who lost promised health benefits

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits group health plans from canceling, cutting, or increasing the cost of retiree health benefits after a participant retires, and voids plan provisions that purport to allow such cuts.
Requires plans to give retirees the option to have benefits that were already reduced after retirement restored, with written notice of what is being restored and its value.

Creates a federal loan guarantee program — capped at $5 billion in guarantees, $5 million per employer — so plan sponsors that cannot afford restoration can borrow from private lenders with a federal guarantee.
Lets the Secretary of Labor assess civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation, per aggrieved retiree, giving the ban real teeth.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that sponsor ERISA group health plans would bear the cost of restoring previously cut benefits and of never cutting them again. The federal government would back up to $5 billion in loans and appropriate $200 million for the guarantee program's costs plus $10 million for administration, putting taxpayers behind loans to struggling plan sponsors.

drawbacks.text: Restoring benefits already taken away would be a retroactive cost for employers, including some facing financial trouble; the bill acknowledges this by allowing hardship waivers and loan guarantees, but the obligation would still fall hardest on companies least able to pay.
Taxpayers would be on the hook if employers defaulted on the federally guaranteed loans, and the $200 million appropriation is designated as emergency spending outside normal budget discipline.

The hardship exemption gives the Labor Secretary broad discretion to waive or delay restoration, and plans with fewer than 100 participants are exempt entirely, so many retirees at smaller employers would get no relief.
The $1,000 per-violation penalty is small relative to the cost of restoring benefits for large employers, which could make the fine a cost of doing business rather than a deterrent.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For retirees who spent their working lives counting on retiree health coverage and lost it after retiring — often because preexisting conditions made replacement coverage unaffordable — the benefit is substantial and targeted. The main costs fall on the employers that made the cuts, and the bill includes real escape valves (hardship waivers, small-plan exemptions, loan guarantees) that limit the burden but also shrink how many retirees get relief. The loan guarantee program is the weakest piece: it spends federal money to help employers finance obligations the bill itself created. On balance the bill is a genuine consumer and retiree protection, weakened by its own exemptions.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, then to its Employer-Employee Relations subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Tierney introduced the Emergency Retiree Health Benefits Protection Act of 2005 in the House on March 15, 2005.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
On April 18, 2005 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations, where it stayed.
79 members cosponsored the bill — 78 Democrats and 1 Independent; no Republicans signed on.
The bill received no further action of any kind and died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and plan sponsors that had cut or canceled retiree health benefits were better off, because the bill's restoration mandate never became law. Retirees who lost benefits got nothing; the protections never took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers that had cut retiree benefits

for.name: Rep. John F. Tierney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and championed protections for retirees whose health benefits were cut after retirement.

for.name: 78 of 202 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it 79 total supporters in the House.

against.name: Rep. John Boehner
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee the bill was assigned to never scheduled a markup or a vote on it, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 79 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's Independent; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled committee and House took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would bar them from cutting retiree health benefits after retirement and force restoration of past cuts, unless they qualified for a hardship waiver. Its death spared them those costs.

Group health plans (including insurer-administered ones) would lose the ability to raise retiree premiums or coinsurance or narrow access to care after retirement. Insurers that kept premiums while cutting what they covered would bear the cost of the locked-in benefits.

The bill would create a federal loan guarantee program backing up to $5 billion in private loans to employers to finance benefit restoration, up to $5 million per sponsor — a new government-backed lending business, though one designed to serve retirees.
